lessons.title: What happens when you open a URL
lessons.sum: Follow one request from the browser to the database and back. Every later topic plugs into this path.

sec.b:
Every system you will design is a variation of this path. Learn it once and each building block has an obvious place.

Browser→DNS→CDN→Load balancer→App servers→Cache→Database
  1. DNS turns shop.com into an IP address. Answers are cached by the browser, the OS and your ISP.
  2. TCP and TLS open a connection and encrypt it. This costs 2 to 3 round trips on a first visit.
  3. CDN serves static files (images, JS) from a server near the user.
  4. Load balancer picks one of many identical app servers.
  5. App server runs your code. It should hold no user state, so any server can handle any request.
  6. Cache and database hold the data. The cache is fast and temporary, the database is the source of truth.

When something is slow or broken, you debug by walking this path. When someone says "add a cache" or "add a queue", you ask where on this path it goes and what it changes.

Habit to build: for any feature, say out loud which of these steps it touches.

breaks: DNS records have a TTL. After a failover, some users keep hitting the old IP until their cached answer expires.
A TLS certificate expires at a fixed minute and takes the whole site down. Automate renewal and alert 30 days early.
A slow client retries and the server sees the same request twice. Writes need to be safe to repeat.
After a deploy the cache is empty, so every request goes to the database at once.

quiz.q: A returning visitor opens shop.com again. Which step can the browser skip without asking any server, because the answer is stored locally?
o: Opening a connection, because connections are kept open forever
The DNS lookup, because the IP address was cached until its TTL ends
Logging in, because the server remembers every browser
The HTTP request, because pages are always cached for a year
quiz.w: DNS answers are cached by the browser and the operating system for the length of their TTL. Connections do close, and the server still has to answer the request.

lessons.title: Networking: TCP, UDP, HTTP and TLS
lessons.sum: How data actually moves between machines, and why connection setup is expensive.

sec.b:
TCP gives you a reliable, ordered stream. UDP just sends packets and leaves reliability to you.

SYN→SYN-ACK→ACK→Data flows
TCPUDP
SetupThree-way handshakeNone
DeliveryReliable, ordered, retransmittedBest effort, may drop or reorder
SpeedSlower start, congestion controlLow latency
Used forWeb, databases, email, file transferDNS, video calls, games, QUIC

• HTTP/1.1 reuses a connection (keep-alive) but handles one request at a time per connection.
  • HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection.
  • HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, which avoids head-of-line blocking at the transport layer.
  • TLS encrypts traffic and proves the server's identity with a certificate. TLS 1.3 needs one extra round trip on a new connection.

A cold connection costs several round trips before the first byte of data. Reusing connections is one of the cheapest speed-ups there is.

breaks: Opening a new connection per request exhausts ports and wastes round trips. Use pooling and keep-alive.
One slow request blocks others on an HTTP/1.1 connection (head-of-line blocking).
Expired certificates take sites down at a fixed minute. Automate renewal.
Long timeouts hide dead connections. Set sensible connect and read timeouts.
DNS lookups add latency to every cold start. Cache and reuse.

quiz.q: A live video call loses a packet. Why is UDP usually a better fit than TCP here?
o: UDP encrypts the stream by default, which TCP is unable to do
UDP guarantees every packet arrives in the right order
UDP keeps working when the Wi-Fi connection is down
A late packet is useless, so dropping it beats stalling everything to resend it
quiz.w: TCP retransmits and delivers in order, so one lost packet delays everything behind it. A call would rather skip a moment than wait.

lessons.title: Processes, threads and storage basics
lessons.sum: How a machine runs your code and keeps your data, which explains most performance surprises.

sec.b:
• A process has its own memory. A crash in one does not corrupt another.
  • Threads inside a process share memory, which is fast but creates race conditions.
  • Context switching between threads costs time, so thousands of busy threads are slower than a few.
  • An event loop (Node.js, async I/O) handles many connections on few threads by never blocking.

TypeWhat it isExamples
BlockRaw disk blocks you format yourselfLocal SSD, cloud volumes
FileShared directory treeNFS, EFS
ObjectWhole objects by key over HTTP, cheap and durableS3, Cloud Storage

RAID combines disks: RAID 0 stripes for speed with no safety, RAID 1 mirrors, RAID 5 and 6 add parity to survive one or two disk failures, RAID 10 mirrors and stripes. The OS keeps hot file data in a page cache in memory, and data is only safe on disk after fsync.

breaks: Thread-per-request designs run out of threads when a dependency is slow.
Skipping fsync is fast until a power cut loses acknowledged data.
RAID is not a backup. It does not protect against deletion or corruption.
Running out of file descriptors or inodes looks like random failures.
A full disk breaks logging, databases and deploys all at once.

quiz.q: Two threads in one process update a shared counter and some updates vanish. Why cannot two separate processes damage each other's memory this way?
o: Each process has its own memory, while threads in one process share it
Processes run on different CPUs, so they never overlap in time
The operating system locks a variable whenever it changes
Processes run more slowly, which hides the timing problem
quiz.w: Threads share one address space, so unsynchronised writes can interleave. Processes are isolated from each other by the operating system.

lessons.title: Latency, throughput and availability
lessons.sum: The few numbers worth memorising, and why averages lie.

sec.b:
OperationRough time
Read from memory (RAM)100 ns
Read from SSD100 µs
Round trip inside one data centre0.5 ms
Round trip across a continent100 to 150 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD1 ms

Memory is about 1,000 times faster than SSD, and a network hop is about 5,000 times slower than memory. That gap is why caches exist and why you avoid chatty services.

TargetDowntime per yearPer month
99.9% (three nines)8.8 hours43 minutes
99.99% (four nines)52 minutes4.3 minutes
99.999% (five nines)5 minutes26 seconds

Components in a chain multiply. Three services in series at 99.9% each give 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.7%. Redundancy (components in parallel) raises availability, dependencies in series lower it.

p50 is the typical request. p99 is the slowest 1 in 100. Users feel the tail. If one page makes 100 backend calls and each has a 1% chance of being slow, then 1 − 0.99100 ≈ 63% of page loads hit at least one slow call.

Always ask for p95 and p99 targets, never just "average latency".

breaks: An average of 80 ms hides a p99 of 4 seconds that is driving users away.
Adding a dependency quietly lowers your overall availability.
Fan-out makes tail latency dominate: the more calls per request, the more often you hit the slow one.

quiz.q: A request passes through three services in a chain, each 99.9% available. About what is the overall availability?
o: 99.9%, since all three services have the same target
About 99.7%, because the availabilities multiply
99.99%, because three checks make failure less likely
About 97%, because each service loses a full percent
quiz.w: 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 0.997. Every dependency in series lowers the total.

lessons.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
lessons.sum: Turn "10 million users" into requests per second, storage and bandwidth in two minutes.

sec.b:
1. Start from daily active users (DAU) and actions per user per day.
  2. Divide by 86,400 seconds for average requests per second (rps). Round to 100,000 seconds to do it in your head.
  3. Multiply by 2 to 3 for peak.
  4. Multiply writes by item size, days and replication factor for storage.
DAU                = 10,000,000
actions / user/day = 10
requests / day     = 100,000,000
average rps        = 100M / 86,400  ~= 1,150
peak rps (x3)      ~= 3,500

new posts / day    = 1,000,000 at 1 KB each
storage / year     = 1M x 1 KB x 365 ~= 365 GB
with 3 replicas    ~= 1.1 TB

The numbers choose the architecture. 1,000 rps fits on one database. 100,000 rps needs caching and sharding. 1 TB fits on one disk. 1 PB does not. You are not after exact figures, only the order of magnitude.

breaks: Designing for the average and falling over at peak, which is often 3 to 10 times higher.
Forgetting replication, indexes and backups, so real storage is 3 to 5 times what you computed.
Ignoring the read to write ratio. A 100:1 read-heavy system wants caches, a write-heavy one wants queues and partitioning.

quiz.q: A service receives 100 million requests a day. About how many requests per second is that on average?
o: About 1,200
About 100, dividing by a million
About 12,000
About 120,000
quiz.w: A day has 86,400 seconds, and 100,000,000 / 86,400 is about 1,157. Peak is usually two to three times higher.

lessons.title: Requirements and trade-offs
lessons.sum: Clarify what to build before drawing boxes, and learn the choices that no design avoids.

sec.b:
• Functional: what must the product do? What is explicitly out of scope?
  • Scale: users, rps, data size, growth.
  • Latency: how fast must key actions feel?
  • Availability vs correctness: is a wrong answer worse than no answer?
  • Consistency: must everyone see the same data instantly?

sec.h: CAP and PACELC in plain words
sec.b:
When the network splits, a distributed system must choose: stay consistent (refuse some requests) or stay available (answer, possibly with stale data). PACELC adds that even with no failure you trade latency against consistency.

DataChooseBecause
Bank balanceConsistencyA wrong balance is worse than a short error
Like counterAvailabilityOff by a few for a second is harmless
Shopping cartAvailabilityNever block someone from adding to cart

breaks: Designing for a billion users when you have a thousand. Cost and complexity arrive first, scale later.
Leaving "consistent" undefined. Ask which data needs it, since most does not.
Missing a hidden requirement such as audit logs, data residency or deletion rules.

quiz.q: You are designing a post's like counter and a bank balance. Which pairing of consistency needs is sensible?
o: Both need strong consistency, because wrong numbers lose trust
Both can be eventually consistent, since users refresh anyway
The counter can be eventually consistent, the balance needs strong consistency
The counter needs strong consistency, the balance can be eventual
quiz.w: A like count that is briefly off is harmless, so favour availability and speed. A wrong balance is worse than a short error.

lessons.title: Load balancing
lessons.sum: Spread traffic across servers, detect failures and deploy without downtime.

sec.b:
Clients→Load balancer→Server A→Server B→Server C

A load balancer (LB) is the front door. It forwards each request to a healthy server, which lets you add servers (scale out) and replace them without users noticing.

TypeWorks onUse for
L4IP and portRaw speed, any TCP traffic
L7HTTP: paths, headers, cookiesRouting /api to one pool and /img to another

• Round robin: simple, fine when requests cost about the same.
  • Least connections: better when requests vary in duration.
  • Consistent hashing: same key goes to the same server, ideal for caches.
  • Weighted: bigger servers get more.

The LB sends periodic health checks and stops routing to servers that fail them.

sec.h: DNS balancing, auto scaling and failover
sec.b:
• DNS load balancing: return several IPs or route by region. Simple, but cached answers react slowly to failures.
  • Auto scaling: add servers when load rises and remove them when it falls. Requires stateless servers and a good health check.
  • Multi-zone and multi-region: spread servers across zones so one data centre failing does not take you down.

breaks: The LB is a single point of failure. Run a pair, or use a managed cloud LB.
Sticky sessions pin a user to one server. Load becomes uneven and the session is lost if that server dies. Keep servers stateless and store sessions in Redis.
A recovering server gets full traffic at once and falls over again. Use slow start.
Deploys cut in-flight requests. Use connection draining so servers finish current work first.
A health check that only returns "200" can pass while the database is down. Check real dependencies, but not so deeply that one slow call removes every server.

quiz.q: Why should app servers behind a load balancer keep no user state on their own disk or memory?
o: It lets the load balancer skip health checks and send traffic anywhere
It makes every request run faster on the server
It removes the need for a database
Any server can handle any request, so servers can be added or lost freely
quiz.w: Stateless servers are interchangeable. That is what lets the load balancer spread traffic and survive a failure.

lessons.title: Caching
lessons.sum: The cheapest way to make a system faster, and the source of its trickiest bugs.

sec.b:
App→Cache (Redis)→Database
PatternHowTrade-off
Cache-asideApp reads cache, on miss reads DB and fills cacheSimple. First read is slow, stale data possible
Write-throughWrite cache and DB togetherAlways fresh, slower writes
Write-backWrite cache, flush to DB laterFast writes, data loss if cache dies
def get_user(user_id):
    key = "user:" + str(user_id)
    data = cache.get(key)
    if data is not None:
        return data                     # hit
    data = db.query_user(user_id)       # miss
    if data is not None:
        cache.set(key, data, ttl=300)   # 5 minutes
    return data

def update_user(user_id, fields):
    db.update_user(user_id, fields)
    cache.delete("user:" + str(user_id))   # invalidate on write
Memory is finite. LRU evicts the least recently used item, LFU the least frequently used. A TTL bounds how stale an item can get. Choose the TTL by asking how wrong the data may be and for how long.

FeatureRedisMemcached
Data typesStrings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streamsStrings only
PersistenceSnapshots and append-only log, optionalNone
ReplicationPrimary and replicas built inNot built in, shard on the client
Atomic operationsMULTI/EXEC, Lua scripts, INCRSimple increment
Pub/subYesNo
Good forSessions, leaderboards, rate limits, timelinesPlain object caching with high churn

Both answer in under a millisecond from memory. Choose Redis when you need data structures or persistence, Memcached for the simplest possible cache.

breaks: Cache stampede: a popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the database together. Use a lock or single-flight per key, and add random jitter to TTLs.
Stale data: the DB changed but the cache did not. Invalidate on write and keep TTLs short for important data.
Cache penetration: requests for keys that do not exist always miss. Cache the "not found" result briefly, or use a Bloom filter.
Hot key: one key gets most of the traffic and overloads one cache node. Replicate it or add a local in-process cache.
Cold start: an empty cache after a restart crushes the database. Warm it up or ramp traffic gradually.

quiz.q: A very popular cache entry expires and thousands of requests reach the database at once. What is this, and what helps?
o: Cache penetration; a Bloom filter for missing keys helps
A hot key; replicating the entry to more nodes helps
A write-back failure; flushing the cache more often helps
A cache stampede; single-flight locking and TTL jitter help
quiz.w: Many concurrent misses on one expired key is a stampede. Penetration is requests for keys that do not exist, and a hot key is steady heavy traffic on one key.

lessons.title: CDN and object storage
lessons.sum: Serve static files from the edge and keep big files out of your app servers.

sec.b:
A content delivery network caches copies of files in many cities. Users download from a nearby edge, which cuts latency and takes load off your servers.

User→Nearest edge→Origin (if miss)

Services such as S3 store files cheaply and durably. For uploads, the app returns a short-lived pre-signed URL and the client uploads straight to storage, so large files never pass through your servers. Big files use multipart upload with resume.

Client→App: get upload URL→Client uploads to S3→S3 event→Worker: resize

breaks: Users see an old JavaScript file after a deploy. Put a content hash in file names (app.3fa91c.js) so each release has a new URL.
Purging the CDN everywhere takes time and can be rate limited. Prefer versioned URLs over purges.
Private content cached at the edge and served to the wrong person. Mark it private or use signed URLs.
Uploading a 2 GB file through the app server ties up connections. Use pre-signed direct upload.
Never trust file names or types from the client. Validate and scan uploads.

quiz.q: You ship a new JavaScript file but users still get the old one from the CDN. What is the cleanest fix that needs no purge?
o: Set the cache lifetime to a few seconds for every file
Serve the file from the app server and skip the CDN
Put a content hash in the file name, so each release has a new URL
Ask users to clear their browser cache after each release
quiz.w: A new hash is a new URL, so nothing stale is ever requested. Short lifetimes throw away the benefit of the CDN.

lessons.title: Queues and asynchronous work
lessons.sum: Take slow work off the request path and absorb traffic spikes.

sec.b:
API→Queue→Workers→Email, resize, report

The API stores the job and answers "accepted" immediately. Workers process it at their own pace. This decouples producers from consumers, smooths spikes and lets work retry.

ToolStylePick when
SQS, RabbitMQTask queueEach job handled once by one worker
KafkaReplayable logMany consumers, ordering, event history

Real systems give at-least-once delivery: a message may arrive twice. So consumers must be idempotent, meaning processing twice has the same effect as once.

def handle(msg):
    if already_processed(msg.id):      # idempotency check
        return
    charge_card(msg.order_id)
    mark_processed(msg.id)             # same transaction as the charge

SystemModelOrderingPick when
KafkaReplayable logPer partitionHigh volume, many consumers, event history, stream processing
RabbitMQBroker with queues and routingPer queueTask queues, flexible routing, RPC-style messaging
SQS and SNSManaged queue and fan-outOptional FIFOServerless apps and simple cloud-native queues
Redis StreamsLightweight logPer streamSmall real-time feeds when you already run Redis
Google Pub/SubManaged topic and subscriptionOptional ordering keysLarge-scale ingestion on Google Cloud

breaks: Duplicates: the worker crashes after the work but before the acknowledgement. Make handlers idempotent.
A poison message fails forever and blocks the queue. Cap retries and move it to a dead-letter queue.
Consumers fall behind and lag grows silently. Alert on queue depth and age.
Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition. Partition by the key that needs order, such as user_id.
An unbounded queue hides overload until memory runs out. Apply backpressure.

quiz.q: A queue delivers each message at least once. What property must a consumer have?
o: Idempotent: handling a message twice has the same effect as once
Synchronous: it must finish before the next message arrives
Stateless: it must remember nothing between messages
Ordered: it must process messages in the order they were sent
quiz.w: A message can arrive twice, for example when a worker crashes before acknowledging. The handler must tolerate that.

lessons.title: Choosing a database
lessons.sum: SQL or NoSQL is the wrong question. Ask about your data and access patterns.

sec.b:
KindExamplesGood for
Relational (SQL)PostgreSQL, MySQLRelated data, transactions, ad hoc queries
Key-valueRedis, DynamoDBLookups by key at huge scale and speed
DocumentMongoDBNested records read as a unit
Wide-columnCassandraMassive writes, time series
SearchElasticsearchFull-text search, filtering
GraphNeo4jDeep relationship queries

ACID (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable) gives safe transactions. BASE systems trade some of that for scale and availability.

Default to PostgreSQL. Move a specific workload elsewhere only when you can name the limit you hit.
Most real products use one relational database as the source of truth, Redis for cache and sessions, object storage for files and a search engine if search matters. Each store does one job.

breaks: Choosing a document store for clearly relational data, then rebuilding joins in application code.
A partition key that sends most writes to one node (a hot partition) while the rest sit idle.
Adding a column to a huge table locks it. Use online migrations.
The N+1 query bug: one query for a list, then one query per item. Load related rows in one query.
Using the database as a queue or a cache, then wondering why it is slow.

quiz.q: An app needs orders, customers and payments, with transactions across them. What is the sensible default store?
o: A key-value store, because lookups are fast
A relational database such as PostgreSQL
A graph database, because the data is related
A search engine, because users will filter orders
quiz.w: Related data with transactional needs is what relational databases are built for. Move a workload elsewhere only when you can name the limit you hit.

lessons.title: Indexing and sharding
lessons.sum: Make queries fast on one machine, then spread data across many.

sec.b:
An index is a sorted lookup structure (usually a B-tree) so the database avoids scanning the whole table. It speeds reads and slows writes, since every write updates each index.

  • Index columns you filter, join and sort on.
  • In a composite index, column order matters: (user_id, created_at) serves "this user's recent items" but not "all items from today".
  • Check with EXPLAIN that the index is used.

When one database cannot hold the data or take the writes, split rows across shards by a shard key.

StrategyIdeaWeakness
Hashhash(key) mod NResharding moves most data
RangeKey ranges per shardHot ranges (newest data)
DirectoryLookup table says whereLookup is a new dependency

Consistent hashing places shards and keys on a ring, so adding a shard moves only about 1/N of the keys.

breaks: A hot shard: one celebrity or tenant produces most traffic. Split that key further or give it its own shard.
Cross-shard joins and transactions are slow or impossible. Choose the key so common queries stay on one shard.
Resharding live data without downtime needs double-writes and careful backfill. Plan it before you need it.
Auto-increment IDs collide across shards. Use UUIDs or Snowflake-style IDs.
A low-cardinality shard key (such as country) cannot spread load evenly.

quiz.q: Why is consistent hashing better than hash(key) mod N when you add a shard?
o: Each key's hash is faster to compute
Only about 1/N of the keys move, instead of nearly all of them
Every shard ends up with exactly the same number of keys
It removes the need to replicate shards
quiz.w: With mod N, changing N changes the home of almost every key. On a ring a new node only takes over a slice.

lessons.title: Search and autocomplete
lessons.sum: Find documents by their words, rank the best ones first and suggest completions as the user types.

sec.b:
A database that scans every row for the words 'red running shoes' gets slower with every product you add. A search engine does the work ahead of time. It builds an inverted index: for each word, a list of the documents that contain it. A query looks up each word, intersects the lists, and ranks what is left.

Documents→Analyzer: split, lowercase, stem→Inverted index→Query→Ranked results

Matching is not enough, the best match must come first. BM25, the default in Lucene, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, scores a document higher when it contains rare query words many times, and discounts very long documents. Filters (price, brand, in stock) and facets (counts per brand) run on separate structures, so they stay fast. Business signals such as sales or freshness are added on top.

Suggestions must appear in a few dozen milliseconds, so they use their own structure: a trie or an index of edge n-grams that maps a typed prefix straight to the most popular completions. Keep the top few completions precomputed for common prefixes, cache them, and wait a moment after the last keystroke (debounce) before sending the request.

The search index is a copy of your data, never the source of truth. Changes reach it through a queue or a change feed, so it lags the database by a moment. Plan for that lag, and for a full rebuild into a new index followed by an atomic switch when the analyzer or the fields change.

Database→Change feed / queue→Indexer→Search index

breaks: The index is behind the database, so a new product is missing from search for a few seconds. Show it on its own page straight away, and accept that search is eventually consistent.
Deep pagination (page 5,000) makes every shard sort and discard thousands of hits. Limit the depth, or use a cursor such as search_after.
The query is analyzed differently from the documents (case, stemming, accents), so obvious matches never hit. Use the same analyzer on both sides.
A very common word or one popular shard becomes a hot spot. Spread documents by id, not by category, and cache the heaviest queries.
Autocomplete sends a request on every keystroke. Debounce, cancel the old request, and cache the answers for common prefixes.
Using the search engine as the only database. It is not built for transactions or strict consistency, so rebuild it from the real store when needed.

quiz.q: Why is a word search on an inverted index fast, even across millions of documents?
o: The word-to-documents lists are built ahead of time, so a query combines short lists
It scans every document in parallel, using many threads on many machines
It keeps the entire database in memory
It only searches the newest documents
quiz.w: The expensive work of splitting text and listing which documents hold each word happens at index time, not at query time.

lessons.title: Replication and consistency
lessons.sum: Copy data for safety and read scale, and understand what you give up.

sec.b:
• Leader and followers: writes go to the leader, reads can go to followers. Most common.
  • Multi-leader: several regions accept writes. Conflicts must be resolved.
  • Leaderless (quorum): with N replicas, write to W and read from R. If R + W > N you read the latest write.

Synchronous replication waits for followers and never loses data but is slower. Asynchronous is fast but followers lag.

Writes→Leader→Follower 1→Follower 2

• Read-your-writes: after posting, you must see your own post.
  • Monotonic reads: time must not appear to go backwards between two reads.
  • Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop.

breaks: A user writes, then reads from a lagging replica and sees nothing. Read your own recent writes from the leader.
Split brain: after a network split two nodes both act as leader and accept writes. Use quorum-based election and fencing.
Async failover loses the writes the leader had not yet sent.
Multi-leader conflicts resolved by "last write wins" silently drop data. Use merge logic or CRDTs.
Backups that were never restored are not backups. Test the restore.

quiz.q: With 5 replicas, which write and read quorum sizes guarantee that a read overlaps the latest write?
o: W = 2 and R = 3, because reads check a majority
W = 3 and R = 2, because writes reach a majority
W = 3 and R = 3, because R + W is greater than N
W = 2 and R = 2, because that is about half
quiz.w: R + W must exceed N. 3 + 3 = 6 is more than 5, but 2 + 3 = 5 and 3 + 2 = 5 are not.

lessons.title: Storage engines: B-trees and LSM-trees
lessons.sum: How databases lay data out on disk, and what that means for reads and writes.

sec.b: Data lives in fixed-size pages arranged as a tree. A write updates the page in place, with a write-ahead log (WAL) first so a crash can be recovered. Reads are fast and predictable. Used by PostgreSQL and MySQL.

Writes go to a WAL and an in-memory table, which is flushed as immutable sorted files (SSTables). Background compaction merges files. Bloom filters let reads skip files that cannot contain a key. Used by RocksDB, Cassandra and HBase.

B-treeLSM-tree
WritesRandom in-place updatesSequential appends, very fast
ReadsOne tree lookupMay check several files
CostWrite amplification from page updatesWrite and space amplification from compaction
Good forRead-heavy and mixed workloadsWrite-heavy workloads

breaks: Compaction cannot keep up, so writes stall and latency spikes.
Deletes in an LSM-tree are tombstones that linger and slow reads.
A random-key B-tree workload causes page splits and fragmentation.
Bloom filters give false positives, so some wasted reads are normal.
Skipping the WAL fsync risks losing the last acknowledged writes.

quiz.q: Which storage engine usually suits a very high rate of writes, and why?
o: An LSM-tree, because it turns random writes into sequential appends
A B-tree, because it updates pages in place with no extra work
A B-tree, because its reads are fastest, so writes finish sooner
An LSM-tree, because it never needs any background work
quiz.w: LSM-trees buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files, paying later with compaction. B-trees do random in-place page updates.

lessons.title: Transactions, MVCC and isolation levels
lessons.sum: What ACID really promises and the anomalies that appear when it is weakened.

sec.b:
LevelPrevents
Read committedDirty reads
Repeatable read / snapshotDirty and non-repeatable reads, often phantoms
SerializableAll anomalies, including write skew

Classic problems: a lost update (two read-modify-writes overwrite each other) and write skew (two doctors both go off call because each saw the other on call).

• MVCC keeps several versions of a row so readers never block writers.
  • Locks (two-phase locking) block conflicting access and can deadlock.
  • Optimistic checks read a version and update only if it is unchanged.
  • Across services use sagas rather than distributed two-phase commit where you can.
-- optimistic update: fails if someone else changed the row
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance + 10, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7;   -- 0 rows updated means retry

breaks: Read-modify-write in application code loses updates. Update atomically in SQL.
Write skew slips past snapshot isolation. Use serializable or explicit locks.
Long transactions hold locks and bloat old row versions.
Deadlocks happen when locks are taken in different orders. Handle the error and retry.
Assuming the default isolation level is serializable. It rarely is.

quiz.q: Two requests each read a balance of 100, add 10 in application code and write it back. The final balance is 110. What happened?
o: A dirty read: one request saw uncommitted data
A phantom read: a new row appeared during a query
Write skew: two requests broke a rule across different rows
A lost update: one write overwrote the other
quiz.w: Both read 100 and both wrote 110, so one deposit vanished. Do the addition inside the database in one atomic statement.

lessons.title: Data modelling: normalise or denormalise
lessons.sum: Design tables and documents around how the data is read.

sec.b:
NormalisedDenormalised
IdeaEach fact stored once, joined when readCopies stored where they are read
ReadsJoins cost timeFast, one lookup
WritesSimple and consistentUpdate every copy
FitsRelational databases, changing queriesDocument and wide-column stores, known access patterns

For one-to-many relations, embed when the children are always read with the parent and stay small. Reference when they are large, shared or change independently.
List your queries first. In NoSQL stores the queries decide the layout. When you duplicate data, keep copies in sync with events or change data capture, and accept that copies may be briefly stale.

breaks: Duplicated data drifts out of sync. Have one owner and propagate changes.
Unbounded embedded arrays make documents huge. Reference instead.
Joins across many tables become slow at scale. Denormalise the hot paths.
Premature denormalisation makes every change harder. Start normalised.
Schema changes on denormalised data need backfills.

quiz.q: A product page always shows the product plus its five photos, and the photos never change on their own. What suits a document store?
o: Keep the photos in their own collection and join on read
Embed the photos inside the product document
Store each photo as a document in a second database
Keep only photo IDs and fetch each photo with its own call
quiz.w: Small child data that is always read with its parent is a good fit for embedding. It needs one lookup and no joins.

lessons.title: Serialisation: JSON, Protobuf and Avro
lessons.sum: Choosing how data is encoded, and keeping old and new code compatible.

sec.b:
JSONProtobufAvro
EncodingTextBinary, field numbersBinary, schema describes order
Size and speedLarger, slowerSmall and fastSmall and fast
SchemaOptionalRequired, in .proto filesRequired, travels with data or a registry
FitsPublic APIs, debuggingService-to-service, gRPCKafka and data pipelines

• Add new fields as optional with defaults.
  • Never reuse or renumber a field.
  • Do not remove a field until no reader depends on it.
  • Use a schema registry to check changes before they ship.

breaks: Removing or renaming a field breaks old readers.
Reusing a Protobuf field number corrupts old data.
JavaScript loses precision on 64-bit integers in JSON. Send them as strings.
Timestamps without a timezone cause off-by-hours bugs.
Huge JSON payloads waste bandwidth. Compress or use a binary format.

quiz.q: Which change keeps old readers of a Protobuf message working?
o: Reusing the number of a removed field for a new field
Changing a field's type from a number to a string
Deleting a field and renumbering the ones after it
Adding a new optional field with a new field number
quiz.w: Old readers ignore fields they do not know. Reusing or renumbering fields makes old data decode as the wrong thing.

lessons.title: Choosing a data store: time-series, wide-column, search, graph, vector
lessons.sum: Match the workload to the store, and keep multiple stores in sync.

sec.b:

RelationalPostgreSQL, MySQLTransactions and joins
Key-valueRedis, DynamoDBFast lookups by key
DocumentMongoDBFlexible records read as a unit
Wide-columnCassandra, HBaseMassive write throughput, time-ordered data
Time-seriesInfluxDB, TimescaleDBMetrics and sensor data with windows

Real systems use several stores. Keep one source of truth, and feed the others through events or change data capture so they can be rebuilt.

breaks: Using a search engine as the primary database. It is a derived index.
Expecting exact results from vector search. It returns nearest neighbours.
High-cardinality tags blow up time-series storage.
Stores drift apart when sync jobs fail silently. Monitor lag.
Adding a new store for one query adds a system to run forever.

quiz.q: A shop uses PostgreSQL plus a search index. Where should the source of truth live?
o: In PostgreSQL, with the index rebuilt from it when needed
In the search index, because it already has every field
In both, written separately by the application
In the cache, because it is the fastest store
quiz.w: An index is derived data and can be rebuilt. Writing to two places separately invites drift between them.

lessons.title: CAP theorem and consistency models
lessons.sum: What you give up when the network splits, and the spectrum of consistency in between.

sec.b:
Partitions happen, so the real choice is what to do during one: stay consistent and refuse some requests (CP), or stay available and risk stale or conflicting data (AP).

SystemLeansNote
etcd, ZooKeeper, HBaseCPMajority quorum
MongoDB (primary reads)CPSingle primary per shard
CassandraAPTunable per query
DynamoDBAPEventual by default, strong reads optional

From strongest to weakest: linearizable (acts like one copy), sequential, causal (cause before effect), read-your-writes, eventual (converges if writes stop). PACELC adds that even with no partition you trade latency for consistency. Quorum reads and writes (R + W > N) let you tune it per query.

breaks: Reading CAP as "pick any two". Partition tolerance is not optional.
Mixing up CAP consistency with ACID consistency.
Ignoring latency. The everyday trade-off is speed vs freshness.
Claiming a system is "CA". A single node is, a distributed system is not.
Using one consistency level for everything. Choose per feature.

quiz.q: During a network partition, what does a CP system do?
o: It accepts writes on both sides and merges them later
It switches to eventual consistency and keeps answering
It shuts down every node until the network is repaired
It refuses some requests on the minority side, to stay consistent
quiz.w: A CP system gives up availability on the side that cannot reach a majority rather than let copies diverge.

lessons.title: Consensus: Paxos and Raft
lessons.sum: How a group of machines agrees on one answer even when some fail.

sec.b: Nodes must agree on a value, such as who the leader is or the next entry in a log, despite crashes and delays. The answer needs a majority quorum: with N = 2f + 1 nodes you tolerate f failures. Three nodes tolerate one failure, five tolerate two. etcd, ZooKeeper and Consul use consensus for leader election, configuration and locks.

Elect leader→Replicate log→Commit on majority→Apply
  • Terms and elections: a follower that hears nothing starts an election after a random timeout and needs a majority of votes.
  • Log replication: the leader appends entries and sends them to followers.
  • Commit: an entry is committed once a majority stores it.
  • Safety: a new leader must hold all committed entries.

Paxos solves the same problem and is harder to read. Raft was designed to be understandable.

breaks: Even-sized clusters add cost without extra fault tolerance. Use 3 or 5.
Losing the majority stops writes. That is safe, not a bug.
Slow disks or long pauses cause repeated elections.
Spreading a cluster across far regions makes every write slow.
Forcing a minority node to lead can lose committed data.

quiz.q: A 5-node Raft cluster loses two nodes. What happens?
o: It stops accepting writes until a node returns
It keeps serving reads but refuses every write
It keeps working, because 3 of 5 is still a majority
It elects two leaders, one for each group
quiz.w: Raft needs a majority. With N = 2f + 1 nodes it tolerates f failures, so five nodes tolerate two.

lessons.title: Clocks and ordering
lessons.sum: Why you cannot trust timestamps across machines, and what to use instead.

sec.b: Each machine has its own clock, kept roughly right by NTP. Clocks differ by milliseconds or more. Ordering writes by wall-clock timestamp ("last write wins") can silently discard the newer write when its server's clock is behind.

• Lamport timestamps: a counter. Increment on each event, send it with messages, and on receive set it to max(local, received) + 1. Gives a consistent order, but cannot tell concurrent events apart.
  • Vector clocks: one counter per node. Show which events are causally related and which are concurrent, so conflicts can be detected and merged.
  • Hybrid logical clocks: wall time plus a counter, close to real time and still ordered.
  • TrueTime (Spanner): exposes clock uncertainty and waits it out to give global ordering.
class Lamport:
    def __init__(self): self.t = 0
    def local_event(self): self.t += 1; return self.t
    def send(self): self.t += 1; return self.t
    def receive(self, remote): self.t = max(self.t, remote) + 1; return self.t

breaks: Last-write-wins on timestamps loses data when clocks are skewed.
Using timestamps as unique IDs causes collisions.
Leap seconds and clock jumps break duration measurements. Use a monotonic clock.
Vector clocks grow with the number of writers. Prune or use dotted version vectors.
Assuming devices have correct clocks. Phones do not.

quiz.q: Two writes to one key came from different servers. Which tool can tell whether they were concurrent?
o: Wall-clock timestamps, because the later time is the newer write
Lamport timestamps, because equal values mean concurrent
The order in which the writes reached the database
Vector clocks, because incomparable vectors mean neither came first
quiz.w: Lamport timestamps give a consistent order but cannot show concurrency. Wall clocks can be wrong by the skew between servers.

lessons.title: API design and rate limiting
lessons.sum: Design interfaces that survive retries, growth and abuse.

sec.b:
• Name resources as nouns: GET /orders/42, POST /orders.
  • Use proper status codes: 201 created, 400 bad input, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 429 too many requests.
  • Paginate every list. Prefer cursor pagination over offset.
  • Version the API (/v1/) so you can change it later.
  • Accept an Idempotency-Key header on anything that moves money or creates things.

AlgorithmIdeaNote
Fixed windowN requests per minute bucketAllows a burst at the window edge
Sliding windowCount over the last 60 sSmoother, more memory
Token bucketTokens refill at a rate, each request spends oneAllows controlled bursts, most popular

breaks: Offset pagination skips or repeats rows when data changes between pages. Use a cursor based on a sorted key.
The client retries a payment after a timeout and the customer is charged twice. Idempotency keys fix this.
Limiting by IP punishes everyone behind one office or mobile network. Limit by user or API key as well.
In a distributed limiter two servers both read "9 of 10 used" and both allow the request. Do the check and increment atomically (Redis Lua or INCR).
Returning 200 with an error body hides failures from monitoring.

quiz.q: A client times out on a payment request and retries. How do you avoid charging twice?
o: Reject every retry with an error, so the client must start over
Raise the timeout so retries become rare
Require an idempotency key and return the saved result for repeats
Charge twice and refund duplicates every night
quiz.w: The server stores the result under the key. A retry with the same key gets the same answer without a second charge.

lessons.sum: Three ways to expose an API, and when each one fits.

sec.b:
RESTGraphQLgRPC

PayloadJSONJSONProtobuf, binary
StrengthSimple, cacheable, universalNo over- or under-fetchingFast, streaming, generated clients
WeaknessChatty for complex screensQuery cost, caching is harderNeeds a proxy for browsers

• Make unsafe operations idempotent.
  • Version the contract and change it compatibly.
  • Paginate lists.
  • Return consistent errors.

breaks: GraphQL resolvers cause N+1 queries. Batch with a data loader.
Unbounded GraphQL queries can be expensive. Limit depth and cost.
Browsers cannot speak gRPC directly. Use gRPC-web or a gateway.
Breaking a Protobuf contract breaks every caller.
REST endpoints that mirror database tables leak internals.

quiz.q: Which API style best suits fast, typed calls between your own backend services?
o: GraphQL, because clients choose their own fields
REST, because every browser can call it
gRPC, with compact Protobuf messages and generated clients
Server-sent events, because they keep a connection open
quiz.w: gRPC is compact, fast and gives typed clients, which suits internal calls. REST and GraphQL suit public and varied clients.

lessons.title: API gateway, service discovery and the strangler fig
lessons.sum: The front door of a microservice system and how to migrate away from a monolith.

sec.b:
Client→API gateway→Service A→Service B

A gateway terminates TLS, authenticates, rate limits, routes and can combine responses. Service discovery lets services find each other as instances come and go: a registry (Consul, Eureka) or the platform itself (Kubernetes DNS).

Put a router in front of the monolith. Move one feature at a time into a new service and route its paths there. When nothing is left, retire the monolith. You always have a working system.

Router→New service (moved paths)→Monolith (the rest)

breaks: A single gateway is a bottleneck and single point of failure. Run several.
Business logic creeping into the gateway makes it a new monolith.
Stale registry entries send traffic to dead instances. Use health checks and short TTLs.
Dual-writing during migration lets data drift. Pick one owner per piece of data.
Every extra hop adds latency.

quiz.q: What is the core idea of the strangler fig pattern?
o: Move features one at a time behind a router until the old system is empty
Rewrite the whole monolith privately and switch on release day
Run two monoliths side by side and let users choose
Replace the database first and the code later
quiz.w: You replace the monolith gradually, and the system keeps working throughout.

lessons.title: Monolith vs microservices
lessons.sum: When to split a system and what it costs you.

sec.b:
One deployable app with clean internal modules is the fastest way to build and the easiest to debug. Split a service out only when a clear reason appears: a team needs to deploy independently, a part needs different scaling, or it needs a different technology.

MonolithMicroservices
DeployOne unitMany small units
DebugOne stack traceDistributed tracing needed
TransactionsDatabase handles themSagas and eventual consistency
Team scaleHard to coordinate once many teams share itFits many teams

Without a shared database you cannot wrap an order, payment and stock change in one transaction. A saga runs each step locally and, if a later step fails, runs compensating actions to undo earlier ones (refund the payment, release the stock).

Create order→Reserve stock→Charge card→Confirm

breaks: A distributed monolith: services that must deploy together and call each other constantly. You get the costs of both styles.
A compensating step fails too. Make compensations idempotent and retry them from a durable log.
Service A deploys a changed response and B breaks. Version APIs and add contract tests.
Chatty services: one page triggers 40 internal calls, so latency and failure odds explode.

quiz.q: A new product is starting with a small team. What is the sensible default architecture?
o: Microservices from day one, so scaling is easy later
One service per database table, for clean ownership
A well-structured monolith, split later for a concrete reason
Serverless functions for everything, to avoid servers
quiz.w: A modular monolith is faster to build and easier to run. Split a service out when a team, a scaling need or a technology demands it.

lessons.title: Event-driven design: pub/sub, CQRS and event sourcing
lessons.sum: Let services react to what happened instead of calling each other directly.

sec.b: With request/response the caller waits. With publish/subscribe a service announces a fact (OrderPlaced) and anyone interested reacts. This decouples teams and absorbs spikes, at the cost of eventual consistency.

• CQRS: separate the model you write to from the models you read from, so each can be shaped and scaled for its job.
  • Event sourcing: store the sequence of events as the source of truth and rebuild state by replaying them. You get a full history and can build new read models later.
  • Outbox pattern: write the event to a table in the same transaction as the data change, then publish it, so you never lose or invent an event.
Command→Write model→Events→Read model→Query

breaks: Duplicate and out-of-order events. Make handlers idempotent and carry versions.
Users see stale read models. Design the UI for eventual consistency.
Event schemas live forever. Evolve them compatibly.
Replaying events can re-trigger side effects like emails. Separate projections from actions.
Writing to the database and publishing separately can lose events. Use an outbox.

quiz.q: Why use the outbox pattern when a service changes data and also publishes an event?
o: It makes events smaller and cheaper to send
It lets the service skip the message broker and write straight to consumers
The change and the event are saved in one transaction, so neither is lost
It guarantees events arrive in exactly the order produced
quiz.w: Writing to the database and publishing separately can lose one of the two. The outbox row commits with the data and a relay publishes it afterwards.

lessons.title: Resilience patterns
lessons.sum: Assume every dependency will be slow or down, and keep the rest alive.

sec.b:
• Timeouts: every network call gets one. No timeout means threads pile up forever.
  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter: wait 1 s, 2 s, 4 s plus a random amount.
  • Circuit breaker: after repeated failures stop calling the dependency for a while and fail fast.
  • Bulkheads: separate pools so one slow dependency cannot use every thread.
  • Graceful degradation: if recommendations fail, still show the page without them.
def call_with_retry(fn, tries=4):
    delay = 0.2
    for attempt in range(tries):
        try:
            return fn(timeout=1.0)
        except TransientError:
            if attempt == tries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(delay + random.uniform(0, delay))
            delay *= 2

breaks: Retry storm: every client retries at once, which keeps the struggling service down. Add jitter and a retry budget.
Retrying non-idempotent calls creates duplicates.
Cascading failure: A waits on slow B, A runs out of threads, then everything that calls A fails.
A circuit that never closes again. Allow a few trial requests (half-open).
Retries at every layer multiply: 3 retries across 3 layers means 27 calls.

quiz.q: Why add random jitter to retry delays?
o: So each retry is faster than the one before
So failed requests are logged less often
So the server can tell retries from new requests
So many clients do not all retry at the same instant
quiz.w: Synchronised retries create a thundering herd that keeps a struggling service down. Jitter spreads them out.

lessons.title: Case: token bucket rate limiter
lessons.sum: Implement the limiter used by most real APIs.

sec.b:
Each client has a bucket of up to capacity tokens. Tokens refill at rate per second. A request spends one token or is rejected with 429. Bursts up to capacity are allowed, sustained traffic is capped at the rate.

import time, threading

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, rate):
        self.capacity, self.rate = capacity, rate
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.last = time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def allow(self):
        with self.lock:
            now = time.monotonic()
            self.tokens = min(self.capacity,
                              self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
            self.last = now
            if self.tokens >= 1:
                self.tokens -= 1
                return True
            return False

limiters = {}   # user_id -> TokenBucket
def check(user_id):
    b = limiters.setdefault(user_id, TokenBucket(10, 5))
    return b.allow()

breaks: Use a monotonic clock. Wall-clock changes can refill or freeze the bucket.
One bucket per user grows memory forever. Expire idle buckets.
Across many servers use shared state, and do refill and spend atomically (a Redis Lua script).
Return 429 with a Retry-After header so well-behaved clients back off.
Fail open or closed when the limiter store is down? Decide on purpose.

quiz.q: What does a token bucket allow that a strict fixed rate does not?
o: A short burst up to the bucket size, with the long-term rate still capped
Unlimited traffic for as long as the bucket still holds any tokens
Different limits for every endpoint with no extra state
Exact counting across many servers with no shared state
quiz.w: Unused tokens accumulate up to the capacity, so a brief burst passes while sustained traffic is limited to the refill rate.

lessons.title: Observability and testing
lessons.sum: Know what is happening in production before users tell you.

sec.b:
SignalQuestion it answersExample
LogsWhat happened?Structured JSON with a request ID
MetricsHow much, how fast?Requests per second, error rate, p99
TracesWhere did the time go?One request across five services

Define SLOs, such as "99.9% of requests succeed and 95% are faster than 300 ms". Alert when you burn the error budget too quickly, not on every blip.

• Unit tests for business rules, many and fast.
  • Integration tests against a real database for repos and APIs.
  • Load tests (k6, Locust) to find the limit before users do.
  • Failure tests: kill a dependency in staging and confirm it degrades gracefully.

breaks: Alert fatigue: too many noisy alerts, so the real one is ignored. Alert on user-visible symptoms.
Metrics labelled by user ID or URL create millions of series and a huge bill.
Personal data in logs becomes a compliance problem.
Only testing the happy path. Test timeouts, duplicates, empty and huge inputs.
Dashboards nobody looks at. Review them in an incident drill.

quiz.q: One user request crosses five services and is slow. Which signal shows where the time went?
o: A distributed trace of that request
The CPU metric of each service
A log line from the first service
The average latency on the main dashboard
quiz.w: A trace follows one request across services and shows the time spent in each hop. Logs say what happened and metrics say how much.

lessons.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
lessons.sum: Turn "reliable" into a number you can plan around.

sec.b:
TermMeaningExample
SLIA measurement of behaviourShare of requests that succeed in under 300 ms
SLOThe target for the SLI99.9% over 30 days
SLAA contract with consequencesRefund if below 99.5%

The budget is what the SLO allows to fail. A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of downtime. A 99.99% SLO allows about 4 minutes. While budget remains you ship quickly. When it is spent, reliability work comes first. Alert on how fast the budget is burning, not on single blips.

breaks: An SLO that is too strict is unaffordable. Match it to what users need.
Measuring on the server misses what users feel. Measure at the edge.
Alerting on causes (CPU) instead of symptoms (errors) creates noise.
No policy for what happens when the budget is spent.
Averages hide the slow tail. Use percentiles.

quiz.q: About how much downtime does a 99.9% SLO allow in a 30-day month?
o: About 4 minutes
About 43 minutes
About 8 minutes
About 7 hours
quiz.w: 0.1% of 30 days is about 43 minutes. A 99.99% SLO allows about 4 minutes.

lessons.title: Chaos engineering and incident response
lessons.sum: Break things on purpose in a controlled way, and run incidents calmly.

sec.b:
1. Define the steady state as a metric, such as orders per minute.
  2. Form a hypothesis: it stays steady if one instance dies.
  3. Inject the failure (kill an instance, add latency) with a small blast radius.
  4. Compare, learn, fix, and widen the experiment.

Netflix popularised this with Chaos Monkey. Run game days to practise together.

• Have an incident commander and a communicator.
  • Mitigate first (roll back, fail over), find the root cause after.
  • Keep a timeline.
  • Hold a blameless postmortem and track the follow-up actions.

breaks: Experiments in production with no abort switch and a huge blast radius.
No steady-state metric, so you cannot tell if it worked.
Fixing the symptom and never the cause.
Blame culture hides the real lessons.
Postmortem actions that nobody owns.

quiz.q: What should you define before injecting a failure into production?
o: The largest failure the system could possibly suffer
A company-wide freeze on deployments
The failure list recommended by the tool vendor
A steady-state metric, a hypothesis and a small blast radius
quiz.w: You need to know what normal looks like, what you expect to happen, and how to limit the damage if you are wrong.

lessons.title: Multi-region and disaster recovery
lessons.sum: Plan for losing a whole data centre or region: how much data you can lose, how fast you recover, and what it costs.

sec.b: Two numbers define a recovery plan. RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can afford to lose, measured in time: 'at most 5 minutes of orders'. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long you can be down: 'back within 30 minutes'. The smaller the numbers, the more the design costs, so agree them with the business first.

Backup and restore is cheapest and slowest, since you rebuild from backups in another region. Pilot light keeps data replicated and the core switched off, ready to scale up. Warm standby runs a smaller full copy that you scale up on failover. Active-active serves traffic from several regions at once, with the shortest recovery and the highest cost and complexity.

Backup and restore→Pilot light→Warm standby→Active-active

Servers are easy to recreate, data is not. Replicating across regions is slower than inside one, so asynchronous replication has a lag (your RPO) and synchronous replication adds latency to every write. Active-active needs a plan for conflicting writes, such as routing each user to a home region. Test restores, because an untested backup is only a hope.

Failover means detecting the problem, deciding to switch, and moving traffic, usually with health checks and DNS or a global load balancer. Automatic failover is fast but can trigger by mistake, so many teams keep a human decision for whole-region failover. Rehearse regularly in game days: only a failover you have done before will work under pressure.

breaks: The backups exist but nobody has ever restored one, and the restore fails or takes a day. Run restore tests on a schedule.
The standby region lacks capacity or quota when everyone fails over at once. Pre-provision, or reserve capacity.
Failover works for the app but the database is hours behind. Monitor replication lag against the RPO.
Automatic failover flips on a brief network glitch and causes the outage it was meant to prevent. Add damping, or a human decision.
Configuration, secrets and DNS records exist only in the primary region. Replicate or define them as code.

quiz.q: What does an RPO of 5 minutes mean?
o: You can lose at most the last 5 minutes of data
Recovery must be complete within 5 minutes
Backups must finish running within 5 minutes
A failure must be detected within 5 minutes
quiz.w: RPO measures how much data you can lose, in time. RTO measures how long you can be down.

lessons.sum: Log users in safely and avoid the common web vulnerabilities.

AttackDefence

IDOR: GET /orders/43 returns someone else's order because only the login was checked. Authorise every object access.
Tokens stored in localStorage can be read by an XSS bug. Prefer httpOnly cookies.
CORS set to * together with credentials exposes user data.
Password reset links that never expire or can be reused.
Logging passwords, tokens or personal data.

o: SQL injection through the order ID in the URL
Missing object-level authorisation (an IDOR bug)
A weak password hashing algorithm
Cross-site scripting in the order page

lessons.title: Network security: TLS, VPCs and zero trust
lessons.sum: Keep data encrypted, keep networks small, and trust nothing by default.

sec.b:
• In transit: TLS everywhere, including between internal services.
  • At rest: encrypted disks and buckets with keys in a key management service, rotated regularly.
  • Networks: a VPC with public subnets for load balancers and private subnets for apps and databases. Security groups allow only the ports and sources needed.

Give each service only the permissions it needs. Zero trust means every request is authenticated and authorised, even from inside the network, often with mutual TLS. Keep secrets in a secrets manager, not in code or images.

Internet→Load balancer (public subnet)→App (private)→Database (private)

breaks: A database or bucket open to the internet.
IAM roles with wildcard permissions.
Long-lived keys committed to a repository.
Unencrypted internal traffic that anyone on the network can read.
No audit log, so you cannot tell what was accessed.

quiz.q: Where should a production database live?
o: In a private subnet reachable only from the app tier
In a public subnet, protected by a strong password
In the same subnet as the load balancer
Anywhere, as long as the traffic uses TLS
quiz.w: Only the app tier needs to reach it, so keep it off the internet. TLS protects data in transit but does not shrink the attack surface.

lessons.title: Containers and Kubernetes
lessons.sum: Package once, run anywhere, and let an orchestrator keep it running.

sec.b: A container packages your app and its dependencies and shares the host kernel, so it is lighter than a virtual machine and starts in seconds. An image is built in layers, so rebuilds are quick.

kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: myorg/api:1.4.2        # pin a version, never "latest"

Using the "latest" image tag makes deployments unrepeatable.
Secrets baked into images.
Running stateful databases in a cluster without a plan for storage.

o: Whether the container should be restarted
Whether the node has enough memory for the pod
Whether the pod should receive traffic from its Service
Whether the image is the latest version
quiz.w: A pod that is not ready is removed from the Service until it passes. Restarts are the job of the liveness probe.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code with Terraform
lessons.sum: Describe your infrastructure in files, review changes, and recreate it on demand.

sec.b:
Write config→terraform plan→Review→terraform apply

You declare the desired state. Terraform compares it to its state file and the real world and shows a plan of changes before doing anything. Reuse patterns through modules.

resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

resource "aws_subnet" "private" {
  vpc_id     = aws_vpc.main.id

}
