  instance_class    = "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage = 20
  username = "app"
  manage_master_user_password = true
  skip_final_snapshot = false
  final_snapshot_identifier = "db-final"
}

• Keep state in a remote backend with locking so two people cannot apply at once.
  • Run plan in code review. Apply from CI.
  • Use separate state for each environment.
  • Watch for drift: changes made by hand in the console.

breaks: A lost or leaked state file. It can hold secrets, so protect and back it up.
Console edits create drift between code and reality.
Applying without reading the plan can destroy a database.
Renaming a resource can mean destroy and create.
One giant state for everything makes every change risky.

quiz.q: What does terraform plan do?
o: Applies the changes after asking for confirmation
Refreshes the state file by deleting stale resources
Checks only the syntax of the configuration files
Shows the changes it would make, without changing anything
quiz.w: Plan is a preview so you can review before you apply.

lessons.title: Serverless and functions
lessons.sum: Run code without managing servers, and know what you trade for it.

sec.b:
You upload a function. The platform runs it on demand, scales it from zero to many copies, and bills per invocation. It suits spiky or event-driven work such as image resizing, webhooks and glue code.

Functions (Lambda)Servers or containers
ScalingAutomatic, to zeroYou configure it
CostPer request and durationPer hour, even when idle
LatencyCold starts on first callAlways warm
LimitsExecution time and concurrency capsFew
StateNone, use external storageLocal state possible
Many parallel functions can overwhelm a database with connections. Use a connection proxy or a queue in between.

breaks: Cold starts add latency to the first request after idle.
Concurrency limits throttle you, and unlimited concurrency floods the database.
A function that triggers itself in a loop produces a huge bill.
Time limits cut off long jobs. Split them or use batch.
Vendor lock-in through triggers and permissions.

quiz.q: Which workload fits functions best?
o: A database that must stay running all day
Resizing an image each time one is uploaded
A job that runs for many hours without a break
A game server holding long-lived connections
quiz.w: Short, event-driven and spiky work is ideal. Long-running or connection-heavy work fits servers or containers better.

lessons.title: Deploying and releasing safely
lessons.sum: Containers, CI/CD, rollouts that can be reversed, and database migrations.

sec.b:
Commit→CI: test + build→Container image→Staging→Production
# Dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

StrategyHowUse when
RollingReplace servers a few at a timeDefault
Blue/greenSwitch traffic between two full environmentsInstant rollback needed
CanarySend 1 to 5% of traffic to the new version firstRisky changes

During a rollout, old and new code run together against the same database. Use expand and contract: first add the new column (code ignores it), then deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only later drop the old column.

breaks: A migration that drops or renames a column breaks the old servers still running during rollout.
No rollback plan. Keep the previous image and make the rollback one command.
A long migration locks a big table. Run in small batches or use online tools.
Config differs between staging and production, so tests pass and prod fails.
Deploying on Friday evening without alerts in place.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to rename a database column in the same deploy that ships new code?
o: Databases cannot rename columns while the app is running
A rename always takes the table offline for hours
Old servers still running during the rollout would break
Renaming is slower than adding a column
quiz.w: Old and new versions overlap during a rollout. Use expand and contract so both versions work at every step.

lessons.title: Scaling from 1 to 1 million users
lessons.sum: The order in which to add building blocks as real load appears.

sec.b:
StageSymptomAdd
1 to 1k usersNoneOne server, one database
Database slow or server busyCPU or disk contentionSeparate DB from app server, add indexes
Single point of failureDowntime during deploys2+ stateless app servers behind a load balancer
Read-heavy loadDB reads dominateCache, then read replicas
Heavy static trafficBandwidth, slow worldwideCDN and object storage
Slow tasks in requestsTimeoutsQueue and workers
Write limit reachedSingle DB cannot keep upPartition or shard, split by domain

Change one thing at a time, measure, and stop when the system meets its targets.

sec.h: Rules to follow on the way
sec.b:
• Fix the slowest query before adding hardware.
  • Keep servers stateless from the beginning, since that is the one thing hard to retrofit.
  • Put numbers behind every addition: "p99 was 900 ms, now 120 ms".

breaks: Sharding too early adds permanent complexity for a problem you do not have yet.
Adding replicas to fix a slow query. Fix the query or index first.
Scaling the app tier while the database stays the single bottleneck.
Stateful servers (files on local disk, in-memory sessions) that block horizontal scaling.
No load test, so the first real test is launch day.

quiz.q: Database reads dominate your load. What do you usually try first?
o: Shard the database across many servers
Move to a different database engine
Add indexes and caching, then read replicas
Add more app servers behind the load balancer
quiz.w: Indexes and caches are cheap and effective. Sharding is a last resort, and more app servers do nothing for a busy database.

lessons.title: Streaming with Kafka
lessons.sum: A replayable log of events, and how consumers scale and fail.

sec.b:
• A topic is split into partitions. Order is guaranteed within a partition only.
  • Each message has an offset. Consumers track how far they have read.
  • A consumer group shares the partitions: each partition goes to one consumer in the group, so parallelism is capped by the partition count.
  • Retention keeps data for a time or size, so consumers can replay.
  • Replication factor copies each partition across brokers.
Producers→Topic partitions→Consumer group→Sink

Frameworks such as Kafka Streams and Flink do windowed counts and joins. Delivery is at-least-once by default. An idempotent producer and transactions give exactly-once within Kafka, but side effects outside Kafka still need idempotent handlers.

# producer: key keeps one user's events in order
producer.send("clicks", key=user_id, value=event)

# consumer in a group: commit only after the work succeeds
for msg in consumer:
    process(msg)            # must be idempotent
    consumer.commit()

breaks: Consumer lag grows silently. Alert on lag and its age.
A bad key sends most traffic to one partition.
Rebalances pause consumption. Avoid frequent restarts.
Too many partitions increase overhead and recovery time.
Retention expires data before a slow consumer reads it.

quiz.q: A topic has 6 partitions and one consumer group. What is the most useful number of consumers in the group?
o: Sixty, because more consumers read faster
Six, because each partition goes to one consumer
One, because a group needs exactly one consumer
Twelve, so each partition has two readers
quiz.w: A partition is read by one consumer in a group, so extra consumers sit idle.

lessons.title: Batch processing, MapReduce and data warehouses
lessons.sum: Process huge datasets in bulk, and store them for analysis.

sec.b:
Map→Shuffle by key→Reduce

Map each record to key-value pairs, shuffle so equal keys meet, then reduce each group. Hadoop MapReduce writes to disk between steps. Spark keeps data in memory and plans a graph of steps, which is much faster. Presto/Trino run SQL across data lakes.

# word count in Spark
counts = (sc.textFile("logs/*")
            .flatMap(lambda line: line.split())
            .map(lambda w: (w, 1))
            .reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b))

A warehouse (Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake) stores data in columns for fast analytics (OLAP), unlike a row-based transactional database (OLTP). ETL transforms before loading, ELT loads then transforms inside the warehouse. A lambda design runs batch and streaming side by side, a kappa design uses streaming alone.

breaks: Data skew leaves one task running for hours.
Thousands of tiny files slow everything. Compact them.
Running heavy analytics on the production database.
Re-running a non-idempotent job duplicates results.
Upstream schema changes silently break pipelines.

quiz.q: Why is a columnar warehouse better than a row-based transactional database for analytics?
o: It has no schema, so any kind of data can be loaded without planning
A query reads only the columns it needs, and columns compress well
It stores less data because it drops old rows
It builds an index on every column automatically
quiz.w: Analytics scans a few columns across many rows. Columnar storage reads just those columns.

lessons.title: SOLID principles
lessons.sum: Five rules that keep classes easy to change.

sec.b:
PrincipleMeaningSmell it fixes
Single responsibilityA class has one reason to changeA class that validates, saves and emails
Open/closedAdd behaviour by adding code, not editingA growing if/elif chain
Liskov substitutionA subclass works anywhere its parent doesA child that throws "not supported"
Interface segregationSmall focused interfacesClasses forced to implement unused methods
Dependency inversionDepend on abstractions, not concrete classesBusiness logic that creates its own database connection

# Before: edit this function for every new discount
def price(order, kind):
    if kind == "student": return order.total * 0.9
    if kind == "vip":     return order.total * 0.8
    return order.total

# After: add a new class, change nothing else
class Discount:
    def apply(self, total): raise NotImplementedError
class Student(Discount):
    def apply(self, total): return total * 0.9
class Vip(Discount):
    def apply(self, total): return total * 0.8

def price(order, discount: Discount):
    return discount.apply(order.total)

breaks: Over-engineering: an interface for a class with one implementation and no tests. Apply the rules when change actually hurts.
God classes that know everything and are touched in every pull request.
Inheritance used for code reuse, so changing the parent breaks every child. Prefer composition.

quiz.q: A function with an if/elif chain that you edit for every new discount type breaks which principle?
o: Liskov substitution: subtypes must replace their parents
Interface segregation: interfaces should be small
Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions
Open/closed: add behaviour by adding code, not by editing it
quiz.w: You should extend behaviour by adding new classes, such as a new discount, instead of modifying existing code.

lessons.title: Modelling with objects
lessons.sum: A repeatable routine for any low-level design round or real feature.

sec.b:
1. Clarify requirements and what is out of scope.
  2. Find entities: the nouns become classes (Vehicle, Spot, Ticket).
  3. Find behaviour: the verbs become methods (park, unpark, pay).
  4. Relate them: is-a (inheritance), has-a (composition), uses (dependency).
  5. Choose patterns only where variation exists (pricing rules, notification types).
  6. Write the core flow first, then handle edge cases.

• Prefer composition over inheritance.
  • Keep data and the behaviour that changes it together.
  • Hide internals. Expose the smallest public surface.
  • Model states explicitly (PENDING, PAID, CANCELLED) and guard the allowed transitions.

breaks: Deep inheritance trees (Vehicle → Car → ElectricCar → TeslaCar) that make changes painful.
Anemic models: classes that are only data bags while all logic lives in one giant service.
Exposing mutable internals, so any caller can put an object into an invalid state.
Primitive obsession: passing raw strings and ints where a small type (Money, Email) would prevent bugs.

quiz.q: In the object-modelling routine, what do the nouns in the requirements usually become?
o: Methods, with the verbs becoming classes
Classes, with the verbs becoming their methods
Design patterns, with the verbs becoming interfaces
Database tables, with the verbs becoming columns
quiz.w: Nouns suggest entities (classes) and verbs suggest behaviour (methods).

lessons.title: Design patterns that matter
lessons.sum: The handful of patterns you will actually use.

sec.b:
Swap an algorithm at runtime. Use it for pricing, routing, payment methods.

class CardPay:
    def pay(self, amount): print("card", amount)
class UpiPay:
    def pay(self, amount): print("upi", amount)

class Checkout:
    def __init__(self, method): self.method = method
    def complete(self, amount): self.method.pay(amount)

Checkout(UpiPay()).complete(499)

Objects subscribe to events without the publisher knowing who they are. Use it for notifications and UI updates.

class OrderEvents:
    def __init__(self): self.subs = []
    def subscribe(self, fn): self.subs.append(fn)
    def publish(self, order):
        for fn in self.subs:
            fn(order)

events = OrderEvents()
events.subscribe(lambda o: print("email", o))
events.subscribe(lambda o: print("update stock", o))
events.publish("order-42")

PatternUse it when
FactoryCreating the right object depends on input (a notifier for email, SMS or push)
StateBehaviour changes with state (order, elevator, vending machine)
DecoratorAdd features by wrapping (logging, caching, retries)
SingletonRarely. It is global state, so prefer passing dependencies in

breaks: Using a pattern because it sounds good. Start with plain code and add a pattern when you feel duplication or rigidity.
Observers that throw an error and stop later subscribers from running. Isolate each callback.
Singletons that make tests share state and fail in random order.
A Factory with a growing switch statement is just the old problem moved. Register creators in a map.

quiz.q: A vending machine behaves differently when idle, holding money or dispensing. Which pattern fits?
o: Singleton: there is only one machine
Decorator: wrap the machine with extra features
State: each state is an object with its own behaviour
Observer: the machine subscribes to coin events
quiz.w: When behaviour depends on the current state, model each state as an object.

lessons.title: Concurrency basics
lessons.sum: Why shared state breaks, and the small set of tools that fix it.

sec.b:
Two threads each do balance = balance + 10. Both read 100, both write 110, and one deposit is lost. Check-then-act on shared data is never safe without protection.

import threading
balance = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def deposit():
    global balance
    for _ in range(100000):
        with lock:                 # remove this lock to see lost updates
            balance += 1

ts = [threading.Thread(target=deposit) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in ts]; [t.join() for t in ts]
print(balance)                     # 400000

• Lock / mutex: one thread at a time in a critical section.
  • Atomic operations: single indivisible updates (INCR in Redis).
  • Optimistic locking: read a version number, update only if it is unchanged, retry otherwise. Good when conflicts are rare.
  • Pessimistic locking: lock the row first. Good when conflicts are common.
  • Thread or worker pools: bound how much runs at once.

breaks: Deadlock: thread 1 holds A and wants B while thread 2 holds B and wants A. Always take locks in the same order.
Holding a lock while doing network or disk I/O stalls everyone behind it.
Check-then-act races, such as "if seat is free then book it". Make it one atomic update.
Lost wake-ups and busy waiting. Use condition variables or queues.
Locks work inside one process only. Across servers, use database locks, versions or a distributed lock with expiry.

quiz.q: Two servers try to book the same seat at the same moment. Which fix works across servers?
o: A mutex inside the booking function on each server
A bigger server so requests finish sooner
A conditional update: set booked only where the seat is still free
A thread-safe in-memory set of booked seats
quiz.w: In-process locks do not span machines. Let the database make the check-and-set one atomic step.

lessons.title: Case: parking lot
lessons.sum: The classic machine-coding problem, with the edge cases that decide the round.

sec.b:
• Multiple levels, spots of sizes small, medium and large.
  • Vehicles: bike, car, truck. A vehicle needs a spot of at least its size.
  • Entry issues a ticket. Exit calculates the fee by time and vehicle type.

ParkingLot→Level→Spot→Ticket→FeePolicy
from enum import IntEnum
import threading, time

class Size(IntEnum):
    SMALL = 1; MEDIUM = 2; LARGE = 3

class Spot:
    def __init__(self, sid, size):
        self.id, self.size, self.free = sid, size, True

class Ticket:
    def __init__(self, tid, spot, plate):
        self.id, self.spot, self.plate = tid, spot, plate
        self.entered = time.time()

class ParkingLot:
    def __init__(self, spots, fee_policy):
        self.spots, self.fee = spots, fee_policy
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
        self.active = {}               # plate -> Ticket
        self.next_id = 1

    def park(self, plate, need: Size):
        with self.lock:                # one thread allocates at a time
            if plate in self.active:
                raise ValueError("already parked")
            for s in self.spots:
                if s.free and s.size >= need:
                    s.free = False
                    t = Ticket(self.next_id, s, plate)
                    self.next_id += 1
                    self.active[plate] = t
                    return t
            raise RuntimeError("lot full")

    def leave(self, plate):
        with self.lock:
            t = self.active.pop(plate)
            t.spot.free = True
            return self.fee.charge(time.time() - t.entered, t.spot.size)

breaks: Two cars are assigned the same spot at the same instant. Allocation must be atomic (the lock above, or a database row lock).
The same plate enters twice without leaving. Reject it or flag a fraud case.
Lost ticket: charge the maximum daily fee and look the car up by plate.
The lot is full. Return a clear error, ideally with the next free time, and never hang.
A truck takes a large spot while small spots sit empty, and then smaller vehicles cannot fit. Choose the smallest spot that fits.
Fee over midnight, daylight saving changes or a server clock change. Store UTC and use a monotonic clock for durations.
Payment fails at exit. Keep the ticket open and the gate closed until paid, or record a debt.

quiz.q: Two entry gates call park() at the same moment. What prevents double allocation?
o: Faster hardware, so requests rarely overlap
Checking for a free spot twice before assigning
Letting the exit gate fix duplicates afterwards
Making check-and-assign atomic with a lock or a row lock
quiz.w: Check-then-assign is a race. It must happen as one indivisible step.

lessons.title: Case: LRU cache
lessons.sum: O(1) get and put with a hash map and a linked list, plus the follow-ups interviewers ask.

sec.b:
A hash map gives O(1) lookup. A doubly linked list keeps items ordered by recency: the most recent at the head, the least recent at the tail. On access, move the node to the head. When full, drop the tail.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, k, v):
        self.k, self.v = k, v
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRU:
    def __init__(self, cap):
        if cap <= 0: raise ValueError("capacity must be positive")
        self.cap, self.map = cap, {}
        self.head, self.tail = Node(0, 0), Node(0, 0)   # sentinels
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _remove(self, n):
        n.prev.next, n.next.prev = n.next, n.prev
    def _add_front(self, n):
        n.next, n.prev = self.head.next, self.head
        self.head.next.prev = n
        self.head.next = n

    def get(self, k):
        n = self.map.get(k)
        if not n: return None
        self._remove(n); self._add_front(n)
        return n.v

    def put(self, k, v):
        if k in self.map:                 # update, do not duplicate
            n = self.map[k]; n.v = v
            self._remove(n); self._add_front(n)
            return
        if len(self.map) == self.cap:
            lru = self.tail.prev
            self._remove(lru); del self.map[lru.k]
        n = Node(k, v); self.map[k] = n; self._add_front(n)

breaks: Updating an existing key must not grow the size or leave a stale node behind.
Capacity 0 or negative. Reject it up front.
Concurrent access corrupts the list. Add a lock, or shard the cache so each shard has its own lock.
Expiry: add a TTL timestamp per node and check it on get.
A single huge item evicts many small ones. Consider size-based weights.

quiz.q: Why does an LRU cache use a doubly linked list instead of a singly linked one?
o: A node can be unlinked in O(1) when you hold a pointer to it
It uses less memory per entry because it stores fewer pointers
It keeps the entries sorted by key
It lets two threads read at once
quiz.w: Removing a node from the middle needs its previous node. A doubly linked list stores that pointer.

lessons.title: Design a URL shortener
lessons.sum: From requirements to a working service: estimates, key generation, redirects and abuse.

sec.b:
• Create a short link for a long URL. Optional custom alias and expiry.
  • Redirect fast and reliably. Reads far outnumber writes.
  • Links should not be guessable in order, and abuse must be handled.

new URLs        = 100M / month  ~= 40 writes/s
read:write      = 100:1        ->  ~4,000 reads/s average, ~12,000 peak
5 years         = 100M x 60    =  6 billion URLs
storage         = 6B x 500 B   ~= 3 TB
key space       = 62^7         ~= 3.5 trillion  (7 chars of a-z A-Z 0-9)

Read-heavy with small data: cache the hot links and one replicated database is enough at first.

POST /v1/links   { "url": "...", "alias": "optional", "expires_at": "optional" }
  -> 201 { "short": "https://sho.rt/aZ3k9Qp" }
GET  /aZ3k9Qp    -> 302 Location: <long url>

table links(code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at)

Client→CDN / LB→Redirect service→Cache→Database
Create API→Key generator→Database

Key generation options:

OptionProsCons
Random 7 charsUnguessableCollisions, so retry on conflict
Base62 of a counterNo collisionsGuessable, counter is a bottleneck
Pre-generated key poolFast, no collisionsExtra service to run

301 vs 302: 301 is cached by browsers, so it is cheaper but you lose click analytics and cannot change the target. 302 sends every click through you.

# pip install fastapi uvicorn  |  run: uvicorn app:app --reload
import secrets, string, sqlite3
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from fastapi.responses import RedirectResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel, HttpUrl

app = FastAPI()
db = sqlite3.connect("links.db", check_same_thread=False)
db.execute("create table if not exists links(code text primary key, url text)")
ALPHABET = string.ascii_letters + string.digits

class In(BaseModel):
    url: HttpUrl

@app.post("/v1/links", status_code=201)
def create(body: In):
    for _ in range(5):                       # retry on collision
        code = "".join(secrets.choice(ALPHABET) for _ in range(7))
        try:
            db.execute("insert into links values(?,?)", (code, str(body.url)))
            db.commit()
            return {"short": "/" + code}
        except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
            continue
    raise HTTPException(503, "try again")

@app.get("/{code}")
def go(code: str):
    row = db.execute("select url from links where code=?", (code,)).fetchone()
    if not row:
        raise HTTPException(404, "unknown link")
    return RedirectResponse(row[0], status_code=302)

Next steps for you: add a Redis cache in front of the lookup, expiry, a per-user rate limit, and click counting through a queue.

breaks: Two random codes collide. The primary key rejects the second, so retry with a new code.
A custom alias is already taken, or is a reserved word like admin. Return 409 and keep a reserved list.
Expired or deleted links should return 410 or 404 and must also leave the cache.
Malicious targets (phishing, malware). Check against a blocklist and rate limit creation.
One viral link hammers one cache key. Replicate hot keys or serve through a CDN.
Click analytics on every redirect adds write load. Send events to a queue and count in batches.
Open redirect abuse and links pointing to your own domain in a loop. Validate the scheme and host.

quiz.q: Why choose a 302 redirect over a 301 for a link shortener?
o: 302 is faster for users because browsers cache it and skip your server
302 is cached forever, which saves bandwidth
Every click passes through you, so you keep analytics and can change the target
301 is not allowed for links to other sites
quiz.w: Browsers cache 301 redirects, so later clicks bypass you and you cannot change where the link goes.

lessons.title: Design a chat app
lessons.sum: Real-time messaging with delivery guarantees, ordering and offline users.

sec.b:
• 1:1 and group chat, real-time delivery, message history.
  • Delivery states: sent, delivered, read.
  • Works across multiple devices and when users are offline.

50M DAU x 40 messages    = 2B messages/day  ~= 23,000 msg/s average
message ~100 B           = 200 GB/day  ~= 73 TB/year, or about 220 TB with 3 replicas
connections              = ~10M concurrent WebSockets
                           at ~50k per server -> ~200 gateway servers

Phone→WebSocket gateway→Chat service→Message store
Chat service→Queue→Push notifications (offline)
  • Gateway: holds the persistent WebSocket per device and is stateless except for the live connection. A registry (Redis) maps user_id to the gateway holding it.
  • Chat service: assigns an ID, stores the message, then delivers to online recipients or pushes a notification.
  • Store: partition by conversation_id so one conversation's messages sit together and are ordered by a sequence number. A wide-column or key-value store fits.

// npm i ws
const { WebSocketServer } = require("ws");
const wss = new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 });
const online = new Map();            // userId -> socket
const seen = new Set();              // client message ids (dedupe)

wss.on("connection", (ws, req) => {
  const user = new URL(req.url, "http://x").searchParams.get("user");
  online.set(user, ws);
  ws.on("message", (raw) => {
    const m = JSON.parse(raw);       // { id, to, text }
    if (seen.has(m.id)) return;      // duplicate from a retry
    seen.add(m.id);
    const dest = online.get(m.to);
    if (dest) dest.send(JSON.stringify({ from: user, text: m.text }));
    else queueForPush(m);            // offline: store and notify
    ws.send(JSON.stringify({ ack: m.id }));
  });
  ws.on("close", () => online.delete(user));
});
function queueForPush(m) { /* save to DB, send push */ }

breaks: The phone loses signal after sending and retries, so the receiver gets the message twice. The client creates a unique message ID and the server dedupes.
Messages arrive out of order. Use a per-conversation sequence number and sort by it.
A user has three devices. Deliver to all and keep read state in sync through the server.
A group of 100,000 members makes one message into 100,000 deliveries. Fan out through a queue and put very large groups on a pull model.
A gateway crashes and 200,000 clients reconnect together. Use jittered reconnect backoff and connection limits.
Presence ("online") flickers on bad networks. Use heartbeats with a grace period.
Users delete messages or accounts. Plan retention, deletion and (if promised) end-to-end encryption early.

quiz.q: A phone resends a message after a timeout. How do you avoid showing it twice?
o: The server ignores any message that arrives after a delay
The client creates a unique message ID and the server dedupes on it
The server sorts by timestamp and drops equal ones
The receiving phone compares the message texts
quiz.w: A stable ID makes the retry recognisable as the same message, whatever its text or timing.

lessons.title: Design a location service (nearby search)
lessons.sum: Find the closest drivers, shops or friends among millions of moving points, quickly.

sec.b: 'Show restaurants within 2 km' or 'find the nearest free driver' cannot be answered by comparing your position with every row. A normal index on latitude alone does not help, because nearby places also differ in longitude. The trick is to turn two-dimensional space into something an index handles well: cells.

A geohash encodes a position as a short string, and places that share a long prefix are close together, so a normal prefix lookup finds a neighbourhood. A quadtree keeps splitting a square into four until each holds only a few points, so crowded cities get small cells and empty oceans stay large. H3 and S2 divide the earth into regular cells with a clean notion of neighbours. In every case the search is: find the user's cell, add the neighbouring cells, then compute exact distances for the few candidates.

Position→Cell id→Candidates in this and nearby cells→Exact distance and sort

Drivers update their position every few seconds, so locations are write-heavy and constantly outdated. Keep the current position in memory (for example Redis geo commands) keyed by cell, expire entries that have not updated, and write only occasional history to disk. Static places such as shops change rarely and can live in an ordinary database with a spatial index.

Partition by cell or by city so that one machine owns each area, and a request touches only one or a few partitions. A dense downtown cell is a hot spot, so split it into smaller cells or give it more machines. Matching a rider to a driver is a separate service that reads this one.

breaks: A search at the edge of a cell misses points just across the border. Always search the neighbouring cells too.
One huge downtown cell takes all the traffic. Use smaller, adaptive cells there.
Writing every location update to a disk database overloads it. Keep live positions in memory and sample the history.
Stale positions from drivers who went offline appear on the map. Give each entry a time to live.
Ranking by straight-line distance ignores rivers and one-way streets. Re-rank the closest candidates by travel time.

quiz.q: Why search the neighbouring cells as well as the user's own cell?
o: Cells are only accurate to a few kilometres
Empty cells are slower to read than full ones
Neighbouring cells keep copies of the same points
A closer point can sit just across the cell border
quiz.w: Cells cut space into pieces with hard borders, so the nearest point can be in the next cell.

lessons.title: Design a news feed
lessons.sum: Fan-out on write vs read, celebrities, ranking and pagination.

sec.b:
• Users follow others and see a feed of their posts, newest or ranked first.
  • Feed loads in under 200 ms. Posting should show up for followers within seconds.

sec.h: Two ways to build a feed
sec.b:
ApproachHowGoodBad
Fan-out on write (push)On post, add its ID to every follower's feed listReads are instantA user with 10M followers means 10M writes
Fan-out on read (pull)On open, fetch recent posts of everyone you follow and mergeNo wasted workSlow reads for users following many accounts
HybridPush for normal users, pull for celebrities and mergeBalancedMore code
Post service→Fan-out workers→Feed cache (Redis lists)→Feed API

CELEBRITY_THRESHOLD = 100_000

def publish(post):
    db.save(post)
    followers = graph.followers(post.author_id)
    if len(followers) < CELEBRITY_THRESHOLD:
        for batch in chunks(followers, 1000):
            queue.send({"post": post.id, "to": batch})   # workers push into feeds
    # celebrities are merged at read time

def push_worker(job):
    for uid in job["to"]:
        redis.lpush("feed:" + str(uid), job["post"])
        redis.ltrim("feed:" + str(uid), 0, 799)          # keep latest 800

def get_feed(uid, cursor=None, limit=20):
    ids = redis.lrange("feed:" + str(uid), 0, 799)
    for celeb in graph.followed_celebrities(uid):
        ids += recent_posts(celeb, limit=20)
    posts = hydrate(sorted_by_time_desc(ids))            # fetch post bodies
    return paginate(posts, cursor, limit)

breaks: A celebrity posts and the fan-out queue takes hours. Use the hybrid model.
A post is deleted or its author blocked. The feed holds only IDs, so filter at read time when hydrating.
A new follow shows nothing from that account. Backfill their recent posts into the feed.
Pushing into feeds of inactive users wastes work. Skip users inactive for 30 days and rebuild on login.
Offset pagination shows duplicates as new posts arrive. Use a cursor (last seen post ID or time).
A cache node dies and feeds vanish. Rebuild from the database on a miss.
Ranking surprises: the same post appears on every refresh. Track seen items.

quiz.q: Why do large feeds use a hybrid push and pull model?
o: Pushing a celebrity's post to millions of feeds is too costly, so it is pulled at read time
Pulling is always faster than pushing, so pushing is kept only as a backup
Pushing removes the need for a feed cache
It keeps every feed in sync with the follower graph
quiz.w: Push works for normal accounts. For huge accounts it is cheaper to merge their posts when a follower reads.

lessons.title: Design an e-commerce platform
lessons.sum: Catalogue, cart, orders and payments, with spikes and failures.

sec.b:
• Browse and search products, cart, checkout, payment, order tracking, notifications.
  • Very read-heavy browsing, write-critical checkout.
  • Flash sales produce big spikes.
10M daily users, 20 page views each  -> 200M reads/day  ~ 2,300 reads/s (peak ~7,000)
2% buy, 200k orders/day              ~ 2.3 orders/s average, 50/s during a sale
product images in object storage behind a CDN

Client→CDN + API gateway→Catalogue, Cart, Order, Payment services
Order service→Queue→Payment worker→Stock + email
  • Catalogue: read-heavy, cached, with a search index.
  • Cart: fast key-value store keyed by user.
  • Order: a relational database with transactions. Place the order, return an order ID at once, and process payment and stock asynchronously.
  • Payment: an external provider behind a circuit breaker with idempotency keys.
  • Checkout as a saga: reserve stock, charge, confirm, with compensation (release stock, refund) on failure.

@app.post("/v1/orders", status_code=202)
def place_order(body: NewOrder, idempotency_key: str = Header(...)):
    existing = db.find_order_by_key(idempotency_key)
    if existing:
        return {"order_id": existing.id}            # safe retry
    order_id = db.insert_order(body, status="PENDING", key=idempotency_key)
    queue.send({"type": "ORDER_PLACED", "order_id": order_id})
    return {"order_id": order_id}                    # fast response

def payment_worker(event):
    order = db.get_order(event["order_id"])
    if order.status != "PENDING":
        return                                       # idempotent
    if reserve_stock(order) and charge(order):
        db.set_status(order.id, "PAID")
    else:
        release_stock(order); db.set_status(order.id, "FAILED")

breaks: Two buyers take the last item. Reserve stock with one atomic conditional update and an expiry.
The payment provider is slow or down. Use a circuit breaker and queue orders.
A customer double-clicks pay. Use idempotency keys.
Payment succeeds but the order write fails. Reconcile with the provider daily.
Held stock is never released when carts are abandoned. Expire holds.
Flash-sale spikes. Rate limit, queue and scale the read path with caching.

quiz.q: Why return an order ID before the payment has finished?
o: It lets the shop skip payment checks for customers it already trusts
Checkout stays fast while slow payment and stock steps run in the background
It avoids storing the order in a database
It guarantees that the payment will succeed
quiz.w: Decoupling keeps checkout fast and absorbs spikes. The order stays PENDING until the workers finish.

lessons.title: Design a notification system
lessons.sum: Send push, SMS and email reliably, once, at the right time, without overwhelming users or providers.

sec.b:
You rarely send messages yourself. Push goes through Apple (APNs) and Google (FCM), SMS and email go through providers such as Twilio or Amazon SES. Your system decides who gets what and when, and hands the delivery to the provider. Each provider has its own limits, formats and failure modes, so put each channel behind its own queue and worker.

Event→Notification service→Queue per channel→Worker→Provider→Device

Before sending, check the user's preferences (opt-outs, quiet hours, channel choice) and fill a template with their language and data. Give messages a priority: a password reset or payment code must not wait behind a marketing campaign of ten million emails, so use separate queues or priority lanes.

Providers fail and time out, so workers retry with exponential backoff. Retrying can send the same message twice, so give every notification an idempotency key and have the worker check it before sending. Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue. Record each state (queued, sent, delivered, opened) so you can answer 'did it go out?'.

A broadcast to ten million users is a fan-out job: split it into batches, spread them over time, and respect provider rate limits. Add per-user limits too, so that one busy day does not send someone fifty pushes. Webhooks from providers report bounces and unsubscribes, which you must honour.

breaks: A retry sends the same message twice. Use an idempotency key checked before every send.
A marketing blast delays urgent one-time codes. Separate queues by priority.
The provider rate-limits you and the queue explodes. Throttle workers to the provider's limit and spread large batches over time.
Messages go to users who opted out or in the middle of the night. Check preferences and quiet hours at send time, not at queue time.
Bounces and invalid device tokens are ignored, so you keep paying to send to dead addresses. Process provider feedback and remove them.

quiz.q: Why give each notification an idempotency key?
o: A retry after a timeout cannot send the same message twice
It encrypts the message on its way to the provider
It lets urgent messages jump the queue
It makes the provider send the message faster
quiz.w: Retries are needed because providers fail, but a retry may repeat a message that did go through. The key lets the worker skip it.

lessons.title: Design a video streaming service
lessons.sum: Upload, encode, store and deliver video to millions, from the edge.

sec.b:
• Upload and play video, with smooth playback on any network.
  • Huge read traffic, heavy bandwidth, global audience.
1M hours watched/hour at ~5 Mbps  -> ~5 Tbps peak egress
 => it must be served from CDN caches near users, not from your origin

Upload→Object storage→Transcoding workers→Many bitrates→CDN edge→Player
  • Transcoding: a fleet of workers splits the video into chunks and encodes each into several resolutions and bitrates.
  • Adaptive streaming (HLS or DASH): the video is cut into a few seconds per segment, and the player switches bitrate as bandwidth changes.
  • Control plane vs data plane: catalogue, recommendations, billing and playback authorisation run as services. The bytes flow from CDN caches placed inside ISP networks (Netflix Open Connect).
  • Resilience: chaos engineering tests that losing instances does not stop playback.

# encode one title into an adaptive HLS ladder with ffmpeg
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 \
  -map 0:v -map 0:a -c:v libx264 -c:a aac \
  -b:v:0 5000k -s:v:0 1920x1080 \
  -b:v:1 2500k -s:v:1 1280x720 \
  -b:v:2 800k  -s:v:2 640x360 \
  -f hls -hls_time 4 -hls_playlist_type vod master.m3u8

breaks: A premiere sends all traffic to a few popular files. Pre-warm the edge caches.
A transcode worker dies mid-job. Make chunks independent and retryable.
A bad network causes buffering. Adaptive bitrate must step down quickly.
Origin overload when many edges miss at once. Use a shield tier between edge and origin.
Piracy and access control need signed URLs and DRM.
Per-title encoding saves bandwidth but adds pipeline complexity.

quiz.q: Why is video served from CDN caches near viewers rather than from one origin?
o: One origin cannot supply terabits per second, and distance adds delay
Encoding video is cheaper at the edge than at a central origin
It avoids needing several bitrates
Origin storage cannot hold video files
quiz.w: Millions of viewers at several megabits each add up to terabits per second, which no single origin can send.

lessons.title: Design a key-value store
lessons.sum: A Dynamo-style store: partitioning, replication, quorums and repair.

sec.b:
• get(key) and put(key, value) at huge scale with low latency.
  • Always writable, tolerant of node loss, easy to add nodes.
  • Tunable consistency.

• Partitioning: consistent hashing with virtual nodes.
  • Replication: each key is stored on N nodes (the next N clockwise).
  • Quorum: write to W, read from R. If R + W > N reads see the latest write.
  • Failures: sloppy quorum with hinted handoff keeps writes going when a replica is down.
  • Conflicts: vector clocks detect concurrent writes so the client or app can merge.
  • Repair: read repair fixes stale replicas on reads, Merkle trees compare data cheaply in the background, and gossip spreads cluster membership.
Client→Coordinator→Replica 1→Replica 2→Replica 3

import bisect, hashlib

class Ring:
    def __init__(self, nodes, vnodes=64):
        self.ring = sorted((self._h(f"{n}#{i}"), n) for n in nodes for i in range(vnodes))
        self.keys = [h for h, _ in self.ring]
    def _h(self, s): return int(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
    def replicas(self, key, n=3):
        i = bisect.bisect(self.keys, self._h(key)) % len(self.ring)
        out, n = [], min(n, len({x for _, x in self.ring}))   # cannot ask for more nodes than exist
        while len(out) < n:                      # next n distinct nodes clockwise
            node = self.ring[i % len(self.ring)][1]
            if node not in out: out.append(node)
            i += 1
        return out

def put(ring, key, value, W=2, N=3):          # nodes are objects with a write(key, value) method
    acks = sum(1 for node in ring.replicas(key, N) if node.write(key, value))
    return acks >= W

breaks: A hot key overloads its replicas. Add a cache or split the key.
Concurrent writes to one key conflict. Use vector clocks and a merge rule.
Adding a node moves data. Stream it in the background.
Hinted handoff data is lost if the stand-in node fails. Keep repairs running.
Clock-based last-write-wins loses writes. Prefer version vectors.
Tombstones for deletes must outlive repairs, or deleted data returns.

quiz.q: A Dynamo-style store keeps 3 replicas of each key. Which write and read quorum sizes guarantee that a read sees the latest write?
o: W = 1 and R = 1, the fastest on both sides
W = 2 and R = 2, because R + W exceeds N
W = 2 and R = 1, because writes reach a majority
W = 1 and R = 2, because reads check a majority
quiz.w: R + W must be greater than N. 2 + 2 = 4 is more than 3, but 2 + 1 = 3 and 1 + 2 = 3 are not.

lessons.title: Design a clickstream analytics pipeline
lessons.sum: Collect millions of events, process them as streams, and query the results.

sec.b:
• Collect page views and clicks from websites and apps.
  • Real-time counters and later ad hoc analysis.
50M DAU x 40 events = 2B events/day  ~ 23,000 events/s (peak ~70,000)
200 bytes each -> 400 GB/day raw

Clients→Collector API→Kafka→Stream processor (Flink or Spark)→Serving store
Kafka→Object storage (raw)→Batch jobs→Warehouse
  • The collector is thin and stateless. It validates and writes to Kafka.
  • Stream jobs count per window and write to a fast store such as Cassandra or an OLAP database.
  • Raw events also go to object storage for reprocessing and the warehouse (a lambda-style design).
  • Use event time with watermarks to handle late events.

# Spark Structured Streaming: clicks per page per minute
clicks = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
    .option("subscribe", "clicks").load()
    .select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("e")).select("e.*"))

counts = (clicks.withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(window("event_time", "1 minute"), "page").count())

counts.writeStream.outputMode("update").format("console").start()

breaks: Late and out-of-order events need watermarks and a clear lateness policy.
Duplicates from retries. Give every event a unique ID and dedupe.
A traffic spike overwhelms the collector. Buffer in Kafka and autoscale.
Bot traffic skews numbers. Filter it early.
Schema changes break jobs. Use a schema registry.
Reprocessing needs idempotent writes.

quiz.q: What does a watermark do in stream processing?
o: It marks repeated events as duplicates so that they are dropped
It sets how long to wait for late events before a window is closed
It encrypts events between Kafka and the processor
It limits how many events each window may hold
quiz.w: It tells the engine when it can stop expecting older events for a window.

lessons.title: How to approach a design interview
lessons.sum: A repeatable framework, plus the design problems mapped to the lessons that cover them.

sec.b:
1. Clarify requirements, users and scale. State what is out of scope.
  2. Estimate traffic, storage and bandwidth.
  3. Define the API and the core data model.
  4. Draw the high-level design and walk one request through it.
  5. Deep dive into the hardest parts: bottlenecks, hot keys, consistency.
  6. Failures and trade-offs: what breaks, how you detect it, what you gave up.

Talk through your reasoning. Say why you chose something and what the alternative costs.

PromptLessons to revisit
URL shortenerCaching, key generation, case study
Chat appWebSockets, queues, case study
News feedFan-out, caching, case study

Codebase in version control, explicit dependencies, config in the environment, backing services as attached resources, separate build and run stages, stateless processes, port binding, scale out through processes, fast startup and graceful shutdown, dev and production alike, logs as streams, admin tasks as one-off processes.

breaks: Jumping to boxes before clarifying what is being built.
Designing for the wrong scale because you skipped estimation.
Listing technologies without saying why.
Ignoring failure. Every component can fail.
Going deep on one part and never finishing the whole design.

quiz.q: What should you do first in a system design interview?
o: Draw the database schema, since data drives the design
Pick a cloud provider and the main technologies
Clarify requirements and scale before drawing anything
Sketch the high-level boxes, then ask questions
quiz.w: Everything else depends on what is being built and how big it is.

lessons.title: From idea to MVP
lessons.sum: Decide what to build first, and what to leave out.

sec.b:
1. Write the core loop in one sentence: who does what and gets which value.
  2. List the nouns and the data (users, items, orders). Design the schema before screens.
  3. Pick boring tools you already know: one language, one framework, PostgreSQL, one host.
  4. Build one vertical slice that works end to end (UI, API, database) before widening.
  5. Cut scope hard. Keep a "later" list. Add logging and basic analytics from day one.
  6. Put it in front of real users early and let their behaviour choose what comes next.

Web app→API→PostgreSQL

A single server and a managed database serve thousands of users. Add the other building blocks from this course one at a time, when a measured problem calls for it.

breaks: Building queues, microservices and Kubernetes before the first user exists.
Starting with screens and discovering the data model does not fit.
No analytics, so you cannot tell which feature people use.
A rewrite halfway through because the first slice was never finished.
Skipping backups on day one because "it is only an MVP".

quiz.q: What should you build first for an MVP?
o: Every feature, hidden behind flags
The admin dashboard, so you can manage users
The scalable architecture you will need later
One thin end-to-end slice of the core loop
quiz.w: A working vertical slice proves the idea and the architecture with the least code.

lessons.title: Building the backend
lessons.sum: Project structure, validation, errors, configuration and migrations.

sec.b:
app/
  main.py          # create app, mount routers
  config.py        # read settings from environment
  routes/          # HTTP only: parse, call service, format response
  services/        # business rules, no HTTP types
  repos/           # database access only
  models.py        # schemas
migrations/        # versioned schema changes
tests/

Keep layers one-directional: routes call services, services call repos. Business rules then stay testable without a web server or a database.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, EmailStr
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException

class NewUser(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)

app = FastAPI()

@app.post("/v1/users", status_code=201)
def create_user(body: NewUser):
    if repo.exists(body.email):
        raise HTTPException(409, "email already registered")
    return repo.insert(body)

• Configuration and secrets come from environment variables, never from the repository.
  • Every schema change is a migration file in version control.
  • Return consistent error shapes with a code and a message.
  • Log a request ID on every line so one request can be followed.

breaks: Trusting client input leads to injection and corrupt data. Validate, and use parameterised queries.
Secrets committed to git stay in history forever. Rotate them and use a secret manager.
Lists without pagination work in testing and time out in production.
The N+1 query bug hides until real data volume arrives.
Business logic in route handlers cannot be reused or tested.

quiz.q: Where should database passwords and API keys live?
o: In a config file that is committed to the repository next to the code
In the front-end code, encrypted with a key
In the Dockerfile, so the image is self-contained
In environment variables or a secrets manager, never in the repository
quiz.w: Anything committed to the repository or shipped to the browser should be treated as public.

lessons.title: Hands-on projects
lessons.sum: Pick projects in any order and spend as long on each as you like. Tick them off when you can show the result.

Skipping measurement. Always record a before and after number.
Building everything at once. Finish one small project before the next.
Never breaking it on purpose. Kill a process and see what happens.

quiz.q: What best shows that you finished a project?
o: You can show a measured result or a working demo
You read all of the instructions
You installed all of the tools
You wrote down what you would build next
quiz.w: A number or a demo that shows the behaviour is the proof. Reading and setup are only the start.
